topics.title: Operating System Structure, System Calls, and User/Kernel Modes
topics.oneLine: The operating system manages hardware resources and provides a secure execution environment using dual-mode operations and system calls.
topics.whyItMatters: Exams test the boundary between user and kernel space, mode transitions, hardware interrupt mechanisms, and system call overhead.
understandSimply: Think of the OS kernel as a bank vault manager.
Applications (user space) cannot enter the vault directly to touch gold bars (hardware memory/devices).
Instead, applications hand a slip (system call) to the manager, who flips a mode switch from User to Kernel, handles the transaction, and returns the result.
technicalExplanation: Dual-mode execution relies on a hardware bit (the Mode Bit) in the Processor Status Word (PSW).
User mode (mode bit = 1) prevents applications from executing privileged instructions (such as disabling interrupts or modifying page tables).
Kernel mode (mode bit = 0) permits full access to hardware and execution of all CPU instructions.
System calls switch execution from user mode to kernel mode via a software trap (or system call instruction like SYSCALL/INT 0x80).
The CPU saves the user context, looks up the trap vector table for the system call handler, executes the handler in kernel mode, sets the mode bit back to 1, and resumes the user process.

definitions.definition: The core component of an OS that always resides in memory and directly controls hardware resources.
A programmatic request by a user program to invoke a privileged service provided by the OS kernel.
A CPU hardware register flag indicating whether current CPU execution is in User Mode (1) or Kernel Mode (0).
A synchronous CPU signal generated by software (e.g. division by zero, system call instruction) to transfer control to the kernel.

steps.title: 1. User Trap Invocation
steps.description: User process sets up system call number/parameters in registers and executes a software trap (e.g. SYSCALL).

steps.title: 2. Hardware Mode Switch
steps.description: CPU hardware automatically saves Program Counter (PC) and PSW, sets Mode Bit to 0 (Kernel Mode), and branches to the Interrupt Vector Table.

steps.title: 3. Kernel Dispatch & Execution
steps.description: Kernel identifies syscall number, validates input parameters, executes requested service (e.g. read file from disk).

steps.title: 4. Return to User Mode
steps.description: Kernel places return code in register, restores user PC/PSW, sets Mode Bit to 1 (User Mode), and resumes user application.

formulasAndMethods: System Call Overhead = Context Switch Latency + Parameter Validation Time + Kernel Handler Execution Time
Mode Bit State: User Mode = 1, Kernel/Supervisor Mode = 0
Trap Vector Lookup: Address = Interrupt Vector Base Register + (Trap Number * Entry Vector Size)

comparisons.title: User Mode vs Kernel Mode Execution
Software Trap vs Hardware Interrupt
rows: Request OS service or handle runtime error
Signal completion of I/O or hardware event

solvedExamples.question: A user program attempts to execute a privileged instruction ('CLI' - clear interrupt flag) while in User Mode (Mode bit = 1). What action is taken by the CPU hardware?
solvedExamples.solution: The CPU hardware detects that Mode bit = 1 while executing a privileged instruction. It prevents execution of the instruction and immediately generates a CPU exception (trap) to transfer control to the OS kernel handler, which typically terminates the offending process with a segmentation/protection fault.

solvedExamples.question: If a system call requires 50 nanoseconds for hardware mode switching and 200 nanoseconds for parameter checking and execution, what is the total time spent in kernel mode per call?
solvedExamples.solution: Total kernel mode time = Mode switch time (to kernel) + Kernel execution time + Mode switch time (back to user) = 50 ns + 200 ns + 50 ns = 300 nanoseconds.

traps: Trap vs Hardware Interrupt: Traps are synchronous (predictable CPU instructions); hardware interrupts are asynchronous (external device signals).
Executing a system call does NOT keep the CPU in User Mode; CPU mode bit switches to 0 during system call handler execution.
System call parameter validation happens inside Kernel Mode to prevent malicious user pointers from corrupting kernel memory.
takeaways: Dual-mode execution enforces protection by restricting privileged operations to Kernel Mode (Mode Bit = 0).
System calls provide the sole interface for user applications to request OS services.
Hardware traps synchronously flip execution mode from User to Kernel.
Hardware interrupts arrive asynchronously from external peripherals.
Monolithic kernels run all core OS services in Kernel Mode, whereas microkernels run servers in User Mode.

quickRecall.question: What is the CPU hardware flag used to distinguish user mode from kernel mode?
quickRecall.answer: Mode Bit (0 for Kernel Mode, 1 for User Mode).

quickRecall.question: Are system calls triggered synchronously or asynchronously?
quickRecall.answer: Synchronously (via software traps/instructions).

quickRecall.question: What happens if a user process executes a privileged instruction in User Mode?
quickRecall.answer: The CPU hardware halts execution and throws a trap/protection exception to the OS kernel.

topics.title: Processes, Threads, Context Switching, and Process State Transitions
topics.oneLine: A process is a program in execution containing its own address space, whereas threads are lightweight units of execution within a process.
topics.whyItMatters: Context switch overhead, PCB vs TCB differences, process state diagrams, and user vs kernel threads are core exam topics.
understandSimply: A process is like a full company office building with its own private land, water supply, and security.
Threads are individual workers inside that office building.
Workers (threads) share the office rooms and desks (code, data, heap), but each worker has their own personal notepad (stack and registers).
technicalExplanation: A process consists of a text section (code), data section (global variables), heap (dynamically allocated memory), stack (local variables, function calls), and a Process Control Block (PCB).
The PCB stores Process ID (PID), Process State, Program Counter, CPU registers, Memory management info (page tables), and Open file lists.
A Process State transitions through NEW -> READY -> RUNNING -> WAITING (BLOCKED) -> TERMINATED.
A Thread (Lightweight Process) shares code, data, heap, and open files with sibling threads, but maintains its own Thread Control Block (TCB), Thread ID, Stack, Program Counter, and Registers.

Context switching between two processes requires saving/restoring entire PCB and flushing/invalidating CPU cache & Memory Management Unit (MMU) TLB entries. Thread switching within the same process retains the address space, reducing context switch latency.

definitions.definition: A kernel data structure holding all administrative info, state, registers, and memory pointers for a specific process.
The state-saving and state-restoring procedure performed by the CPU scheduler when switching execution from one process/thread to another.
A thread managed entirely by a user-space library without kernel awareness; fast to switch but blocks all process threads if one makes a blocking syscall.
A thread managed directly by the OS kernel; scheduling is individual, but thread creation and management incur kernel syscall overhead.

steps.title: 1. Save Current Execution Context
steps.description: CPU saves current process's Program Counter, status registers, and general-purpose registers into its PCB.

steps.title: 2. Update Process State
steps.description: Scheduler changes current process state from RUNNING to READY (if preempted) or WAITING (if requesting I/O).

steps.title: 3. Select Next Process
steps.description: OS CPU scheduling algorithm selects a target READY process from the ready queue.

steps.title: 4. Restore Target Context & MMU
steps.description: Load target process's PCB register values, update page directory base register (CR3 in x86), and switch execution to target PC.

formulasAndMethods: Process Memory Layout: Address Space = Text + Data + Heap (grows upward) + Stack (grows downward)
CPU Utilization with N processes having I/O wait fraction p: $ \text{CPU Utilization} = 1 - p^n $
Context Switch Overhead Percentage = (Context Switch Time / Total Slice Time) * 100

comparisons.title: Process vs Thread
rows: Shares address space, data & code with parent process

comparisons.title: User-Level Threads (ULT) vs Kernel-Level Threads (KLT)
rows: Managed directly by Operating System kernel
Very fast; no kernel mode transition
One thread blocking syscall blocks entire process
Kernel schedules another thread if one blocks

solvedExamples.question: A system has 4 processes running concurrently. Each process spends 70% of its time waiting for I/O operations (p = 0.7). What is the CPU utilization according to the degree of multiprogramming model?
If a CPU context switch takes 5 microseconds and the time quantum in Round Robin scheduling is set to 45 microseconds, what percentage of CPU time is wasted on context switching?
solvedExamples.solution: Total time per slot = Time Quantum + Context Switch Time = 45 us + 5 us = 50 us.\nWasted CPU Time Percentage = (5 us / 50 us) * 100 = 10%.

traps: A process in the WAITING state cannot move directly to RUNNING; it must first transition to READY when its I/O completes.
Threads share global variables and heap, but NEVER share their execution stacks or register sets.
In User-Level Threads (Many-to-One model), if one thread makes a blocking system call, the OS kernel blocks the entire process.
takeaways: PCB stores process metadata and CPU context state.
Process State transitions: RUNNING -> WAITING (I/O request), WAITING -> READY (I/O complete), RUNNING -> READY (Timer interrupt).
Threads within the same process share code, data, heap, and open file descriptors.
Switching threads in the same process does not invalidate TLB/page tables, whereas process context switches do.
Multiprogramming CPU utilization is modeled by 1 - p^N.

quickRecall.question: Can a process move directly from WAITING state to RUNNING state?
quickRecall.answer: No. It moves from WAITING to READY, then the scheduler selects it for RUNNING.

quickRecall.question: Do threads of the same process share memory stack areas?
quickRecall.answer: No. Each thread has its own private stack.

quickRecall.question: What CPU register is updated during a process context switch to switch virtual address space in x86?
quickRecall.answer: Page Directory Base Register (CR3 register).

topics.title: Inter-Process Communication (Shared Memory & Message Passing)
topics.oneLine: IPC enables independent processes to exchange data and synchronize actions via shared memory segments or kernel message passing.
topics.whyItMatters: Comparing IPC mechanisms, message buffering models (blocking vs non-blocking), and circular buffer math are frequently examined.
understandSimply: Imagine two neighbours needing to talk.
Shared Memory is like placing a shared whiteboard on their common boundary wall; both write and read directly.
Message Passing is like using the postal system; messages are handed to a postman (kernel buffer) who delivers them to the recipient.
technicalExplanation: Shared Memory establishes a common region of physical memory mapped into the virtual address space of multiple processes.
Once established, communication occurs at hardware memory speeds without kernel intervention; synchronization (e.g. via semaphores) must be handled by user software.
Message Passing provides explicit primitives: send(destination, message) and receive(source, message).
In Direct Communication, processes explicitly name each other (e.g. send(P, msg)). In Indirect Communication, messages are sent to and received from shared mailboxes/ports.
Synchronization mode can be Blocking (Synchronous: send blocks until received; receive blocks until msg arrives) or Non-blocking (Asynchronous: send resumes immediately; receive returns msg or null).

definitions.definition: An IPC mechanism where processes communicate by reading/writing to a shared region of virtual address space.
An IPC model where processes exchange structured messages through kernel-managed message queues or pipes.
A state achieved when both message sender and receiver use blocking primitives (zero-capacity buffer).
A unidirectional byte stream IPC channel provided by Unix OS (Ordinary/Anonymous Pipe or Named Pipe / FIFO).

steps.title: 1. Shared Memory Creation
steps.description: Process A calls shmget()/shm_open() to request a shared memory segment from the OS kernel.

steps.title: 2. Memory Attachment
steps.description: Processes A and B call shmat() to map the shared physical memory region into their local virtual memory pages.

steps.title: 3. Direct Data Access
steps.description: Process A writes data into the shared array; Process B reads it directly without OS system calls.

steps.title: 4. User-Space Synchronization
steps.description: Processes use Mutex/Semaphores to prevent race conditions during concurrent reads and writes.

formulasAndMethods: Producer-Consumer Shared Array Index (Size N): in = (in + 1) % N; out = (out + 1) % N;
Buffer Empty Condition: in == out
Buffer Full Condition (when using N-1 capacity method): (in + 1) % N == out

comparisons.title: Shared Memory vs Message Passing
rows: Needed only during initial region setup
Needed for every message send and receive

comparisons.title: Direct vs Indirect Message Communication
rows: Processes explicitly name each other (send(P, msg))
Messages sent to shared mailboxes (send(A, msg))
Link can connect multiple processes to one mailbox
Decoupled; allows multiple producers and consumers

solvedExamples.question: A bounded buffer of size N = 8 uses shared memory for producer-consumer IPC. If 'in' = 6 and 'out' = 2, how many items are currently present in the buffer?
solvedExamples.solution: Number of items = (in - out + N) % N = (6 - 2 + 8) % 8 = 4 items.

solvedExamples.question: In a blocking message passing system with a buffer capacity of 0 (zero capacity), process P calls send(Q, msg) at t = 10ms. Process Q calls receive(P, msg) at t = 25ms. At what time does Process P unblock and resume execution?
solvedExamples.solution: With zero capacity buffer, send is blocking until receiver receives the message (Rendezvous). Process P blocks at t = 10ms and remains blocked until Q calls receive at t = 25ms. P unblocks and resumes at t = 25ms.

traps: Shared memory is faster than message passing for large data because it avoids copy operations into kernel buffers.
Zero-capacity buffer in message passing enforces Rendezvous (both sender and receiver block until message handoff occurs).
Anonymous pipes in Unix are unidirectional and can only be used between parent and child processes.
takeaways: IPC mechanisms fall into two main paradigms: Shared Memory and Message Passing.
Shared memory requires explicit user synchronization (semaphores/mutexes).
Message passing handles synchronization in the kernel but incurs system call copy overhead.
Blocking send + Blocking receive creates a strict Rendezvous.
Named pipes (FIFOs) allow IPC between unrelated processes on the same machine.

quickRecall.question: Which IPC model has lower overhead for high-volume data transfers on a local system?
quickRecall.answer: Shared Memory.

quickRecall.question: What is it called when both sender and receiver block until a message is delivered?
quickRecall.answer: Rendezvous (Zero-capacity buffer).

quickRecall.question: Can anonymous Unix pipes be used for IPC between two unrelated processes?
quickRecall.answer: No. Anonymous pipes require parent-child relationship; unrelated processes must use Named Pipes (FIFOs).

topics.title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms (FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Round Robin, Priority)
topics.oneLine: CPU scheduling selects a process from the ready queue to allocate CPU time, optimizing turnaround, waiting, and response times.
topics.whyItMatters: Calculating Turnaround Time, Waiting Time, Response Time, and drawing Gantt charts for preemptive/non-preemptive algorithms is a guaranteed numerical exam section.
understandSimply: FCFS is a queue at a grocery store checkout (first come, first served).
SJF is serving the customer with 1 item before the customer with a full shopping cart.
Round Robin is giving every customer 2 minutes at the counter before sending them to the back of the line if not finished.
technicalExplanation: CPU scheduling metrics:
Turnaround Time (TAT) = Completion Time (CT) - Arrival Time (AT).
Waiting Time (WT) = Turnaround Time (TAT) - Burst Time (BT).
Response Time (RT) = Time of First CPU Allocation - Arrival Time (AT).
First-Come, First-Served (FCFS): Non-preemptive. Suffers from Convoy Effect (short processes waiting behind long ones).
Shortest Job First (SJF): Non-preemptive. Mathematically proves minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes.
Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF): Preemptive version of SJF. Checks remaining burst time whenever a new process arrives.
Round Robin (RR): Preemptive using a Time Quantum (q). If quantum is too large, RR degrades to FCFS; if too small, context switch overhead dominates.
Priority Scheduling: Allocates CPU to highest priority process (can be preemptive or non-preemptive). Can suffer from Starvation (solved via Aging).

definitions.definition: Phenomenon in FCFS where short CPU processes wait behind a long CPU-bound process, lowering CPU/device utilization.
Scheduling where the OS can interrupt a running process to allocate the CPU to another process.
A condition where a ready process is indefinitely delayed from getting CPU execution due to low priority or long jobs.
A technique to prevent starvation by gradually increasing the priority of processes that wait in the ready queue for long durations.

steps.title: 1. Record Arrival & Burst Times
steps.description: Construct a process table with Arrival Time (AT) and Burst Time (BT) for each process.

steps.title: 2. Construct Gantt Chart
steps.description: Trace CPU execution tick-by-tick from t = 0, applying algorithm selection rules (e.g. pick lowest remaining burst time in SRTF).

steps.title: 3. Find Completion Times
steps.description: Mark the exact time tick (CT) when each process finishes its final CPU burst on the Gantt chart.

steps.title: 4. Calculate Metrics
steps.description: Compute TAT = CT - AT and WT = TAT - BT for every process, then take averages.

formulasAndMethods: Turnaround Time: TAT = CT - AT
Waiting Time: WT = TAT - BT = CT - AT - BT
Response Time: RT = First_Execution_Time - AT
Throughput = Total Completed Processes / Total Execution Time

comparisons.title: SJF Non-Preemptive vs SRTF Preemptive
rows: Running process completes its entire CPU burst
Preempts if a newly arrived process has shorter burst
Evaluates burst length only when CPU is free
Evaluates remaining time on every new process arrival
Potentially higher for short arriving jobs
Optimal average waiting time for interactive workloads

comparisons.title: FCFS vs Round Robin
rows: Non-preemptive (CPU held until exit or I/O)
Severe (short processes wait behind long ones)

solvedExamples.question: Consider 3 processes P1, P2, P3 arriving at t=0 with burst times 24ms, 3ms, and 3ms under FCFS. Calculate average Waiting Time.
Processes P1 (AT=0, BT=7) and P2 (AT=2, BT=4) run under SRTF (Preemptive SJF). At what time does P1 complete?
solvedExamples.solution:
At t=0, P1 starts (remaining BT=7).
At t=2, P2 arrives (BT=4). Remaining BT of P1 at t=2 is (7 - 2) = 5.
Since P2's BT (4) < P1's remaining (5), P2 preempts P1.
Points: P2 runs from t=2 to t=6 (completes at t=6).
P1 resumes at t=6 and runs for remaining 5ms (from t=6 to t=11).
P1 Completion Time (CT) = 11.

traps: Waiting Time formula is TAT - BT = CT - AT - BT. Do NOT forget to subtract Arrival Time!
SJF produces the minimum average waiting time among all scheduling algorithms for a fixed set of processes.
As time quantum q approaches infinity, Round Robin becomes identical to FCFS.
takeaways: TAT = CT - AT; WT = TAT - BT.
FCFS suffers from the convoy effect.
SJF (Non-preemptive) gives optimal minimum average waiting time.
SRTF is the preemptive variant of SJF.
Aging resolves starvation in Priority/SJF algorithms.

quickRecall.question: Which scheduling algorithm yields the provably minimal average waiting time?
quickRecall.answer: Shortest Job First (SJF) / SRTF.

quickRecall.question: What is the formula for Process Turnaround Time?
quickRecall.answer: TAT = Completion Time - Arrival Time (CT - AT).

quickRecall.question: What technique is used to eliminate starvation in priority scheduling?
quickRecall.answer: Aging (gradually increasing process priority while waiting).

topics.title: Process Synchronization: Critical Section Problem, Semaphores, and Mutex
topics.oneLine: Process synchronization prevents race conditions when concurrent processes access shared resources by enforcing mutual exclusion.
topics.whyItMatters: Petersons algorithm, counting vs binary semaphores, wait/signal operations, and critical section criteria appear in every OS exam.
understandSimply: Imagine a single-person trial room in a clothing store.
Mutual Exclusion means only 1 person is inside the trial room at a time.
A Semaphore is like a key rack at the counter holding N keys; you take a key to enter and return it when leaving.
technicalExplanation: A Race Condition occurs when multiple processes access and manipulate shared data concurrently, and the final outcome depends on the particular order of execution.
The Critical Section Problem requires a solution satisfying three strict criteria:
1. Mutual Exclusion: If process Pi is executing in its critical section, no other process can execute in their critical section.

2. Progress: If no process is in its critical section and some wish to enter, only those processes not in their remainder section can participate in deciding who enters next, and this decision cannot be postponed indefinitely.

3. Bounded Waiting: There must be a bound on the number of times other processes are allowed to enter their critical sections after a process has made a request to enter and before that request is granted.
Peterson's Solution is a software solution for two processes using `flag[2]` and `turn` variables.
A Semaphore S is an integer variable accessed only through two atomic operations: wait(S) [or P(S)] and signal(S) [or V(S)].
Counting Semaphore: S initialized to N (allows N concurrent accesses).
Binary Semaphore (Mutex): S initialized to 1 (enforces strict 0 or 1 mutual exclusion).

definitions.definition: A flaw where concurrent execution outputs vary unreliably depending on CPU execution interleaving.
A segment of code accessing shared variables or resources that must be executed mutually exclusively.
An OS synchronization primitive maintained as an integer and modified atomically via wait() and signal().
A lock where a process repeatedly checks a condition in a loop (busy waiting) until it acquires access.

steps.title: 1. Entry Section
steps.description: Process executes entry protocol (e.g. wait(S) or sets Peterson flags) to request permission to access critical section.

steps.title: 2. Critical Section
steps.description: Execute critical code accessing shared memory/resources mutually exclusively.

steps.title: 3. Exit Section
steps.description: Execute exit protocol (e.g. signal(S) or clear Peterson flag) to release access for waiting processes.

steps.title: 4. Remainder Section
steps.description: Resume non-critical execution independent of shared resources.

formulasAndMethods: Peterson's Entry Code for Process i (j = 1-i): flag[i] = true; turn = j; while (flag[j] && turn == j);
Atomic wait(S) operation: wait(S) { while (S <= 0); S--; } (or block CPU process)
Atomic signal(S) operation: signal(S) { S++; } (or wakeup blocked process)

comparisons.title: Counting Semaphore vs Binary Semaphore (Mutex)
rows: Manages multiple instances of a resource
Enforces mutual exclusion for a single resource
Must be unlocked by the thread holding the lock

comparisons.title: Busy Waiting (Spinlock) vs Block-Wakeup Semaphore
rows: Continuously loops in CPU while waiting
Suspends process to WAITING state; frees CPU
No context switch cost; wastes CPU cycles
Context switch cost on block and wakeup
Long wait durations or single-processor systems

solvedExamples.question: A counting semaphore S is initialized to 7. Then 12 wait(S) operations and 5 signal(S) operations are executed on S in some arbitrary order. What is the final value of S?
solvedExamples.solution: Final Value = Initial Value - (Number of wait operations) + (Number of signal operations)\nFinal Value = 7 - 12 + 5 = 0.

solvedExamples.question: If a counting semaphore has a current value of -4 in a block-wakeup implementation, what does the negative number indicate?
solvedExamples.solution: In block-wakeup semaphore implementations, a negative value -K indicates that the resource count is exhausted and exactly K processes are currently blocked in the semaphore queue waiting for a signal(). Here, 4 processes are blocked.

traps: In wait(S), decrement happens AFTER the resource is available (S > 0), performed atomically.
Busy waiting consumes CPU cycles; block-wakeup puts the process into the OS WAITING state.
Peterson's solution requires software execution under sequential memory consistency (can fail on out-of-order modern hardware CPUs without memory barriers).
takeaways: Critical Section solutions MUST satisfy Mutual Exclusion, Progress, and Bounded Waiting.
Race conditions occur when shared memory reads/writes interleave unsafely.
Semaphores provide atomic wait(P) and signal(V) primitives.
Counting semaphore value = Initial - Wait + Signal.
Negative semaphore value in block-wakeup indicates the number of blocked waiting processes.

quickRecall.question: What three conditions must be satisfied by any solution to the Critical Section problem?
quickRecall.answer: Mutual Exclusion, Progress, and Bounded Waiting.

quickRecall.question: What is the result of executing 4 wait() operations on a counting semaphore initialized to 3?
quickRecall.answer: The first 3 succeed (semaphore becomes 0), and the 4th blocks the process.

quickRecall.question: Does Peterson's solution require special hardware hardware instructions?
quickRecall.answer: No. It is a pure software solution for two processes.

topics.title: Classic Synchronization Problems (Producer-Consumer, Readers-Writers, Dining Philosophers)
topics.oneLine: Classic synchronization problems benchmark concurrency constructs like semaphores, mutexes, and monitors.
topics.whyItMatters: Questions test semaphore initialization values, deadlock scenarios, and reader vs writer priority logic.
understandSimply: Producer-Consumer: A baker places fresh bread on a shelf (buffer); buyers take bread. Baker stops when shelf is full; buyers wait when shelf is empty.
Readers-Writers: Multiple people can read a newspaper concurrently; but an editor writing the news needs exclusive access (no readers, no other writers).
Dining Philosophers: 5 philosophers sit around a table with 5 chopsticks; each needs 2 chopsticks to eat, illustrating multi-resource allocation deadlock.
technicalExplanation: Producer-Consumer (Bounded Buffer): Uses three semaphores: `mutex = 1` (binary lock for buffer access), `empty = N` (counting space left), `full = 0` (counting items available).
Producer does: wait(empty); wait(mutex); [add item]; signal(mutex); signal(full);
Consumer does: wait(full); wait(mutex); [remove item]; signal(mutex); signal(empty);
CRITICAL RULE: The counting semaphore check (wait(empty)/wait(full)) MUST occur BEFORE wait(mutex). Reversing them causes immediate deadlock when buffer is full/empty!

Readers-Writers Problem: Reader process acquires `mutex` to update `readcount`. If `readcount == 1`, reader executes `wait(wrt)` to lock out writers. When leaving, if `readcount == 0`, reader executes `signal(wrt)`.

Dining Philosophers Problem: 5 processes sharing 5 semaphores `chopstick[5]`. If all pick up left chopstick simultaneously (`wait(chopstick[i])`), all block waiting for right chopstick (`wait(chopstick[(i+1)%5])`) causing Deadlock. Solutions include: allowing at most 4 philosophers at table, or pick chopsticks in asymmetric order.

definitions.definition: Synchronization problem involving a producer writing to a fixed-size buffer and consumer reading from it.
Concurrency pattern balancing simultaneous reads with exclusive write access to shared datasets.
Classic benchmark representing multi-resource allocation issues, deadlock, and starvation.
A high-level synchronization language construct that automatically guarantees mutual exclusion inside its methods.

steps.title: 1. Initialize Semaphores
steps.description: Set binary mutex = 1, counting semaphores (empty = N, full = 0).

steps.title: 2. Producer Sequence
steps.description: Wait on empty space -> Lock mutex -> Insert item -> Unlock mutex -> Signal full item.

steps.title: 3. Consumer Sequence
steps.description: Wait on full item -> Lock mutex -> Extract item -> Unlock mutex -> Signal empty space.

steps.title: 4. Verify No Deadlock Order
steps.description: Ensure counting semaphore wait calls precede binary mutex wait calls.

formulasAndMethods: Producer Semaphore Init: mutex = 1, empty = N, full = 0
Producer Code: P(empty); P(mutex); append(); V(mutex); V(full);
Consumer Code: P(full); P(mutex); take(); V(mutex); V(empty);
Deadlock condition order trap: P(mutex); P(empty); -> CAUSES DEADLOCK!

comparisons.title: Readers-Writers: First Variant vs Second Variant
rows: No reader waits unless a writer holds the lock
New readers wait if a writer is waiting to write

comparisons.title: Semaphore vs Monitor
rows: High-level language construct with implicit mutex
Condition variables with wait() and signal()

solvedExamples.question: In a Producer-Consumer system with buffer size N=5, what are the initial values of semaphores `mutex`, `empty`, and `full`?
solvedExamples.solution: mutex = 1 (binary semaphore for buffer mutual exclusion),\nempty = 5 (counting semaphore representing 5 free slots),\nfull = 0 (counting semaphore representing 0 available items).

solvedExamples.question: A developer writes the producer code as: `wait(mutex); wait(empty); produce(); signal(mutex); signal(full);`. What bug is introduced when the buffer becomes full (empty = 0)?
solvedExamples.solution: When buffer is full (empty = 0), producer executes `wait(mutex)` and succeeds (mutex becomes 0). Next, producer calls `wait(empty)` and blocks because empty = 0. However, producer holds `mutex` = 0. Now consumer tries to execute `wait(full)` and then `wait(mutex)`, but blocks on `mutex` held by producer. Both processes are blocked forever, causing Deadlock.

traps: Reversing `wait(empty)` and `wait(mutex)` in Producer code creates Deadlock when the buffer fills up.
Multiple readers can read simultaneously in the Readers-Writers problem; readers do NOT lock out other readers.
In Dining Philosophers, if all philosophers acquire their left chopstick first, a circular wait deadlock occurs.
takeaways: Producer-Consumer uses `empty=N`, `full=0`, `mutex=1`.
Counting wait MUST precede binary mutex wait.
First Readers-Writers problem privileges readers and can starve writers.
Monitors streamline mutual exclusion compared to error-prone low-level semaphores.
Dining Philosophers illustrates deadlock prevention techniques (e.g. asymmetric resource acquisition).

quickRecall.question: What is the initial value of the `full` counting semaphore in Producer-Consumer with buffer size N?
quickRecall.answer: 0 (zero).

quickRecall.question: What happens if a producer executes `wait(mutex)` BEFORE `wait(empty)` on a full buffer?
quickRecall.answer: System enters Deadlock.

quickRecall.question: Which synchronization construct enforces mutual exclusion at compile time?
quickRecall.answer: Monitor.

topics.title: Deadlocks: Characterization, Prevention, Avoidance, and Detection
topics.oneLine: A deadlock occurs when a set of processes are blocked because each holds a resource and waits for another resource held by another process.
topics.whyItMatters: Banker's algorithm safety sequence, Coffman conditions, and deadlock prevention vs avoidance rules are heavy exam topics.
understandSimply: Imagine 4 cars arriving at a 4-way single-lane intersection simultaneously, each turning right.
Car A blocks Car B, Car B blocks Car C, Car C blocks Car D, and Car D blocks Car A.
None can move forward until a car backs up (releasing its resource).
technicalExplanation: Deadlock requires all 4 Coffman conditions to hold simultaneously:
1. Mutual Exclusion: At least one resource must be non-sharable.
2. Hold and Wait: A process must hold at least one resource and wait for additional resources held by others.
3. No Preemption: Resources cannot be forcibly taken from a process; they are released only voluntarily.
4. Circular Wait: A closed chain of processes exists ($P_0 \to P_1 \to \dots \to P_n \to P_0$) where each process waits for a resource held by the next.
Deadlock Prevention: Disables at least 1 of the 4 Coffman conditions (e.g. impose total ordering on resources to break Circular Wait).
Deadlock Avoidance: Dynamically inspects resource requests. Uses Banker's Algorithm to check if granting a request leaves the system in a Safe State.
Safe State: System can allocate resources to each process in some sequence (Safe Sequence) without causing deadlock.
Banker's Algorithm Matrices:
Need[i][j] = Max[i][j] - Allocation[i][j].
Safety Algorithm maintains Work vector (initialized to Available) and Finish[i] boolean array.

definitions.definition: A permanent state where two or more processes are unable to proceed because each is waiting for resources held by the other.
The four necessary and sufficient conditions for deadlock: Mutual Exclusion, Hold & Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait.
A system state where there exists at least one safe execution sequence that allows all processes to finish without deadlocking.
A directed graph with Process nodes and Resource nodes; a cycle in RAG is a necessary condition for deadlock (and sufficient if single instance per resource).

steps.title: 1. Calculate Need Matrix
steps.description: Compute Need[i][j] = Max[i][j] - Allocation[i][j] for all processes i and resource types j.

steps.title: 2. Initialize Work and Finish
steps.description: Set Work = Available (vector of free resource instances) and Finish[i] = false for all processes.

steps.title: 3. Find Eligible Process
steps.description: Find an index i such that Finish[i] == false and Need[i] <= Work. If no such i exists, jump to Step 5.

steps.title: 4. Reclaim Resources & Repeat
steps.description: Set Work = Work + Allocation[i], Finish[i] = true, and loop back to Step 3.

steps.title: 5. Safety Evaluation
steps.description: If Finish[i] == true for all i, system is in a Safe State (Safe Sequence found). Otherwise, system is Unsafe.

formulasAndMethods: Need Matrix: Need[i] = Max[i] - Allocation[i]
Resource Conservation: Total[j] = Available[j] + Sum(Allocation[i][j])
Deadlock Prevention Rule for Single Instance Resources: RAG cycle => Deadlock
Minimum resources R required to guarantee deadlock-free operation for N processes each needing max K instances: R >= N * (K - 1) + 1

comparisons.title: Deadlock Prevention vs Deadlock Avoidance
rows: Static rules invalidating 1 of 4 Coffman conditions
Dynamic checks analyzing safe states at allocation time
Higher resource utilization using Banker's algorithm
No future resource request information needed
Requires prior knowledge of maximum resource demands

comparisons.title: Safe State vs Unsafe State
rows: At least one safe execution sequence exists
No safe sequence exists for worst-case requests
Deadlock is possible if max requests occur

solvedExamples.question: A system has 3 processes each requiring up to 4 units of a resource R. What is the minimum number of units of R needed to ensure deadlock will NEVER occur?
solvedExamples.solution: To guarantee no deadlock, allocate each process max-1 resources, plus 1 extra overall.\nMinimum resources R = N * (K - 1) + 1 = 3 * (4 - 1) + 1 = 3 * 3 + 1 = 10 units.

solvedExamples.question: In a system with Available = [3, 3, 2], process P0 has Allocation = [0, 1, 0] and Max = [7, 5, 3]. Calculate P0's Need vector and check if Need <= Available.
solvedExamples.solution: Need[P0] = Max[P0] - Allocation[P0] = [7-0, 5-1, 3-0] = [7, 4, 3].\nComparing Need [7, 4, 3] with Available [3, 3, 2]:\nFor resource 1, Need (7) > Available (3). Therefore, P0 cannot be satisfied immediately.

traps: An Unsafe State is NOT identical to a Deadlock; an unsafe state simply means the system *might* deadlock if processes request their maximum declared resources.
In a Resource Allocation Graph (RAG) with multiple instances per resource type, a cycle is a NECESSARY condition but NOT a sufficient condition for deadlock.
Need = Max - Allocation. Never calculate Need as Allocation - Max!
takeaways: Deadlock requires all 4 Coffman conditions.
Deadlock Prevention breaks 1 condition statically.
Banker's Algorithm calculates Need = Max - Allocation and finds a Safe Sequence.
Formula for min deadlock-free resources: R >= N*(K-1) + 1.
A cycle in RAG guarantees deadlock ONLY if resources have single instances.

quickRecall.question: What are the 4 Coffman conditions required for deadlock?
quickRecall.answer: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, Circular Wait.

quickRecall.question: Is an unsafe state in Banker's algorithm guaranteed to be a deadlock?
quickRecall.answer: No. It means deadlock is possible, but not guaranteed.

quickRecall.question: What is the formula for the Need matrix in Banker's Algorithm?
quickRecall.answer: Need[i] = Max[i] - Allocation[i].

topics.title: Memory Management: Contiguous Allocation, Paging, and Segmentation
topics.oneLine: Memory management allocates physical RAM to processes using contiguous partitioning, fixed paging, or dynamic segmentation.
topics.whyItMatters: Paging address translation math, page table size calculations, and internal vs external fragmentation distinction are core exam topics.
understandSimply: Contiguous partitioning is like reserving a block of adjacent seats in a cinema.
Paging breaks a book into fixed 4KB pages; pages can be stored anywhere in physical memory frames.
Segmentation divides a program into logical chapters (main function, stack, library) of variable sizes.
technicalExplanation: Contiguous Memory Allocation assigns a single continuous block of physical memory to each process. Dynamic partitioning algorithms include First-Fit (first big hole), Best-Fit (smallest fitting hole), and Worst-Fit (largest fitting hole).
Fragmentation Types:
Internal Fragmentation: Unused memory space WITHIN an allocated fixed-size block/page.
External Fragmentation: Total free memory space is sufficient to satisfy a request, but it is non-contiguous (split into small scattered holes).
Paging divides logical memory into fixed-size blocks called Pages, and physical memory into same-size blocks called Frames.
Logical Address consists of Page Number (p) and Page Offset (d).
Logical Address Space size = $2^m$ bytes; Page size = $2^n$ bytes => Offset $d = n$ bits; Page number $p = m - n$ bits.
Page Table maps Page Number (p) to Frame Number (f). Physical Address = $(f × Page Size) + d$.
Segmentation divides logical memory into variable-length Segments (Code, Stack, Heap). Segment Table holds Base address and Limit length.

definitions.definition: A non-contiguous memory scheme dividing logical memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into fixed-size frames.
Wasted space occurring inside an allocated block when process data is smaller than the fixed frame size.
Wasted memory occurring when free memory exists in small non-contiguous fragments across physical RAM.
A kernel data structure storing mapping entries between a process's logical page numbers and physical frame numbers.

steps.title: 1. Extract Page Number & Offset
steps.description: Given logical address A and Page Size $2^n$, compute Offset $d = A \pmod{2^n}$ and Page Number $p = \lfloor A / 2^n \rfloor$.

steps.title: 2. Lookup Frame Number
steps.description: Index the process Page Table at entry $p$ to obtain Physical Frame Number $f$.

steps.title: 3. Physical Address Construction
steps.description: Combine Frame Number $f$ and Offset $d$: Physical Address = $(f × 2^n) + d$ (or bitwise concatenate $f \parallel d$).

steps.title: 4. Memory Access
steps.description: Read/write the physical RAM byte at computed Physical Address.

formulasAndMethods: Page Size = 2^n bytes => Offset d = n bits
Logical Address Bits (m) = Page Number Bits (p) + Offset Bits (d)
Number of Pages = Logical Address Space Size / Page Size = 2^(m - n)
Page Table Size = Number of Pages * Page Table Entry (PTE) Size
Physical Address = (Frame Number * Page Size) + Offset

comparisons.title: Paging vs Segmentation
rows: Reflects user/compiler view of program structure

comparisons.title: First-Fit vs Best-Fit Memory Allocation
rows: Allocates the first hole large enough
Searches entire list for smallest hole large enough
Slower allocation due to full list search
Leaves remaining hole usable for other requests

solvedExamples.question: A system uses 32-bit logical addresses and 4 KB page size. If a Page Table Entry (PTE) takes 4 bytes, what is the size of the single-level page table for a process?
solvedExamples.solution:
Page Size = 4 KB = 2^12 bytes => Offset (d) = 12 bits.
Logical Address = 32 bits => Page Number (p) = 32 - 12 = 20 bits.
Number of Pages = 2^20 entries.
Page Table Size = Number of Pages * PTE Size = 2^20 * 4 bytes = 4 MB.

solvedExamples.question: Given a page size of 1 KB (1024 bytes), logical address 3500 maps to which page number and offset?
solvedExamples.solution: Page Number = floor(3500 / 1024) = 3.\nOffset = 3500 mod 1024 = 3500 - (3 * 1024) = 3500 - 3072 = 428.\nLogical address 3500 corresponds to Page 3, Offset 428.

traps: Offset $d$ remains EXACTLY THE SAME in both logical address and physical address in paging.
Paging completely eliminates External Fragmentation, but STILL suffers from Internal Fragmentation on the last page.
In segmentation, if Offset $d ≥ Limit$, a Segmentation Fault exception is raised.
takeaways: Offset bits $d = \log_2(Page Size)$.
Physical Address = $(f × Page Size) + d$.
Paging suffers from internal fragmentation; segmentation suffers from external fragmentation.
Page Table Size = Number of Pages $×$ PTE Size.
Offset $d$ is untouched during page-to-frame address translation.

quickRecall.question: Does standard Paging eliminate internal fragmentation or external fragmentation?
quickRecall.answer: Paging eliminates external fragmentation (leaves internal fragmentation on the final page).

quickRecall.question: If page size is 8 KB (8192 bytes), how many bits are used for the offset in a logical address?
What is the physical address corresponding to Frame 5, Offset 100, with 1KB page size?

topics.title: Virtual Memory: Demand Paging, Page Table Structures, and TLB
topics.oneLine: Virtual memory provides the illusion of an arbitrarily large main memory using demand paging and hardware Translation Lookaside Buffers (TLB).
topics.whyItMatters: Calculating Effective Access Time (EAT) with TLB hit ratios and multi-level page table sizes are standard high-weight GATE/IOCL exam problems.
understandSimply: Demand paging is like streaming a movie.
You don't download all 50 GB before playing; you load 5-second video chunks (pages) into RAM as you watch.
A TLB is a fast cache on the actor's desk storing their top 10 most recent phone numbers so they don't walk to the filing cabinet (main RAM) every time.
technicalExplanation: Demand Paging loads pages into physical RAM frame memory ONLY when accessed during process execution (Lazy Swapper).
When a process accesses a page marked invalid in the Page Table, a Page Fault exception occurs.

Page Fault Handling Sequence: Traps to OS -> Saves process state -> Locates page on backing disk -> Finds free RAM frame -> Issues disk I/O read -> Updates Page Table entry valid bit -> Restores process state -> Restarts faulted instruction.
Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB): A high-speed associative hardware cache inside the CPU MMU that stores recent (Page Number -> Frame Number) mappings.
Effective Access Time (EAT) with TLB hit ratio $h$, TLB access time $t_{tlb}$, and RAM access time $m$:
$EAT = h · (t_{tlb} + m) + (1 - h) · (t_{tlb} + 2m)$ (for single-level page table).
Hierarchical (Multi-level) Paging splits large page tables into smaller page tables so that page tables themselves can be paged out.
In a $k$-level page table, a TLB miss requires $k$ RAM accesses to fetch the frame number.

definitions.definition: A technique separating user logical memory from physical memory, allowing processes larger than physical RAM to execute.
An interrupt generated by MMU hardware when a process accesses a page not currently resident in physical RAM.
A fast associative hardware CPU cache used to speed up logical-to-physical address translation.
A page table structure containing one entry per physical memory frame rather than one entry per logical page.

steps.title: 1. Search TLB Cache
steps.description: CPU searches page number p in hardware TLB associative memory in parallel.

steps.title: 2. TLB Hit Path
steps.description: If p found in TLB (TLB Hit), immediately retrieve Frame f and generate physical address in 1 CPU cycle.

steps.title: 3. TLB Miss Path
steps.description: If p not in TLB (TLB Miss), access Page Table in RAM (requires k memory accesses for k-level table), insert entry into TLB.

steps.title: 4. Page Fault Check
steps.description: If Page Table entry valid bit == 0, trigger Page Fault trap to OS to bring page from disk.

formulasAndMethods: EAT with TLB: EAT = h * (t_tlb + m) + (1 - h) * (t_tlb + (k + 1) * m) [for k-level page table]
EAT with Page Fault Rate p: EAT = (1 - p) * m + p * (Page Fault Service Time)
Inverted Page Table Entries = Total Physical RAM Frames (independent of virtual memory size)

comparisons.title: Single-Level vs Multi-Level Page Table
rows: Entire page table must be contiguous in RAM
Outer table points to inner paged tables
Huge contiguous space required for 64-bit systems
Hierarchical structure saves memory for unmapped regions
1 memory access per page table lookup
K memory accesses for K-level page table

comparisons.title: Standard Page Table vs Inverted Page Table
rows: One dedicated page table per active process
One global page table for the entire system
Indexed by Frame Number (searched by PID + VPN)
Proportional to Virtual Address Space size

solvedExamples.question: A system has a TLB access time of 10 ns and main memory access time of 100 ns. If the TLB hit ratio is 90% and a single-level page table is used, what is the Effective Access Time (EAT)?
solvedExamples.solution:
TLB Hit Time = 10 ns + 100 ns = 110 ns.
TLB Miss Time = 10 ns + 100 ns (page table read) + 100 ns (data read) = 210 ns.
EAT = h * (Hit Time) + (1 - h) * (Miss Time)
EAT = 0.90 * 110 ns + 0.10 * 210 ns = 99 ns + 21 ns = 120 ns.

solvedExamples.question: Memory access time is 200 ns and average page fault service time is 8 milliseconds (8,000,000 ns). What is the maximum acceptable page fault rate p to maintain Effective Access Time under 220 ns?

traps: On a TLB miss with a 2-level page table, accessing memory requires 3 memory references in total (2 for page table levels + 1 for actual data).
Page fault service time is measured in MILLISECONDS (disk access), while RAM access time is in NANOSECONDS. Units must be converted during calculations!
Inverted Page Table size depends on PHYSICAL memory size, NOT virtual address space size.
takeaways: TLB hit reduces memory translation to 1 hardware clock cycle.
EAT = $h(t_{tlb} + m) + (1-h)(t_{tlb} + (k+1)m)$ for $k$-level paging.
Page fault triggers instruction restart after fetching page from disk.
Inverted page tables scale with physical RAM frames.
Demand paging loads pages only upon reference.

quickRecall.question: How many main memory accesses are needed on a TLB miss in a 3-level paging system?
quickRecall.answer: 4 accesses (3 for page table levels + 1 for actual data).

quickRecall.question: What happens to the faulted instruction after a page fault service completes?
quickRecall.answer: The instruction is restarted from the beginning.

quickRecall.question: Does an Inverted Page Table size increase when virtual address space grows?
quickRecall.answer: No. It scales strictly with physical RAM frames.

topics.title: Page Replacement Algorithms (FIFO, Optimal, LRU, Clock) and Thrashing
topics.oneLine: Page replacement algorithms select which resident page to evict when RAM frames are full, aiming to minimize total page faults.
topics.whyItMatters: Tracing page fault reference strings for FIFO, Optimal, LRU, Belady's Anomaly, and thrashing mechanics are classic exam questions.
understandSimply: Imagine a bookshelf (RAM frames) holding 3 books.
FIFO replaces the oldest book put on the shelf.
LRU replaces the book that hasn't been opened for the longest time.
Optimal replaces the book that won't be opened for the longest time in the future (requires magic foresight!).
technicalExplanation: When physical RAM frames are full and a page fault occurs, the OS must select a victim page to evict to disk.
First-In, First-Out (FIFO): Evicts the page that was brought into memory earliest. Suffers from Belady's Anomaly (increasing frame allocation can INCREASE page faults!).

Optimal Page Replacement (OPT / Belady's Algorithm): Evicts the page that will not be used for the longest period of time in the future. Theoretical benchmark yielding the absolute minimum page faults.

Least Recently Used (LRU): Evicts the page that has not been referenced for the longest time in the past. Approximates Optimal by relying on past temporal locality. Belady's anomaly CANNOT occur in LRU (LRU is a Stack Algorithm).
Clock Algorithm (Second Chance): Uses a circular queue of frames and a 1-bit Reference Bit. If reference bit = 1, clear to 0 and advance pointer; if reference bit = 0, evict page.
Thrashing occurs when a process spends more time paging (swapping pages in/out of disk) than executing instructions. Caused when Total Allocation < Working Set Size.

definitions.definition: The counter-intuitive phenomenon where increasing the number of allocated physical frames increases the number of page faults (occurs in FIFO).
A class of page replacement algorithms (e.g. LRU, Optimal) where the set of pages in N frames is always a subset of pages in N+1 frames.
The set of pages referenced by a process in the most recent delta time units, representing its active locality.
A severe performance degradation state where CPU utilization drops to near zero because RAM is overcommitted and disk paging I/O dominates.

steps.title: 1. Read Reference String
steps.description: Take page reference sequence (e.g. 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4) and set frame array size N.

steps.title: 2. Check Frame Residence
steps.description: If reference page is in frame array -> HIT (no fault). Update metadata (e.g. timestamp for LRU).

steps.title: 3. Handle Frame Miss
steps.description: If page not present -> PAGE FAULT. If free frame exists, place page in free frame.

steps.title: 4. Apply Replacement Rule
steps.description: If frames full, apply algorithm rule: FIFO (oldest load), LRU (oldest reference), OPT (furthest future reference).

formulasAndMethods: Page Fault Rate = Total Page Faults / Total References
Belady's Anomaly Condition: Faults(N + 1 frames) > Faults(N frames) [Applies to FIFO]
Working Set Model Thrashing Prevention: Sum(Working Set Size_i) <= Total Physical RAM Frames

comparisons.title: FIFO vs LRU Page Replacement
rows: Replaces the page loaded earliest into memory
Replaces the page unused for the longest time
Requires hardware counters or stack tracking

comparisons.title: LRU vs Optimal Page Replacement
rows: Looks backward in time at past page references
Looks forward in time at future page references
Minimum possible page fault rate for any sequence

solvedExamples.question: For the reference string '1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5' with 3 frames under FIFO, how many page faults occur?
solvedExamples.solution:
Trace FIFO with 3 frames:
Ref 1: [1, -, -] (Fault 1)
Ref 2: [1, 2, -] (Fault 2)
Ref 3: [1, 2, 3] (Fault 3)
Ref 4: Evict 1 -> [4, 2, 3] (Fault 4)
Ref 1: Evict 2 -> [4, 1, 3] (Fault 5)
Ref 2: Evict 3 -> [4, 1, 2] (Fault 6)
Ref 5: Evict 4 -> [5, 1, 2] (Fault 7)
Ref 1: Hit [5, 1, 2]
Ref 2: Hit [5, 1, 2]
Ref 3: Evict 1 -> [5, 3, 2] (Fault 8)
Ref 4: Evict 2 -> [5, 3, 4] (Fault 9)
Ref 5: Hit [5, 3, 4]
Total Page Faults = 9.

solvedExamples.question: Does Belady's Anomaly occur in the LRU (Least Recently Used) page replacement algorithm?
solvedExamples.solution: No. Belady's Anomaly CANNOT occur in LRU because LRU belongs to the class of Stack Algorithms. For any stack algorithm, the set of pages resident in N frames at any point is guaranteed to be a subset of the pages resident in N+1 frames. Therefore, increasing frames can never increase page faults.

traps: Belady's Anomaly affects FIFO, but NEVER affects LRU or Optimal.
Optimal page replacement requires future knowledge of reference string, making it impossible to implement in real OS kernels.
Thrashing causes CPU utilization to DROP sharply (not increase) because processes are constantly blocked waiting for disk page swaps.
takeaways: OPT gives provably minimum page faults using future knowledge.
LRU looks backward in time; it is a Stack Algorithm immune to Belady's anomaly.
FIFO can suffer from Belady's anomaly.
Clock algorithm provides a low-overhead 1-bit approximation of LRU.
Thrashing occurs when total working set size exceeds physical RAM capacity.

quickRecall.question: Can Belady's Anomaly occur in the LRU page replacement algorithm?
quickRecall.answer: No. LRU is a stack algorithm and is immune to Belady's Anomaly.

quickRecall.question: Which page replacement algorithm provides the theoretical minimal page fault rate?
quickRecall.answer: Optimal Page Replacement (OPT / Belady's Algorithm).

quickRecall.question: What happens to CPU utilization during system thrashing?
quickRecall.answer: CPU utilization drops drastically near zero.

topics.title: Disk Scheduling (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK) and I/O Management
topics.oneLine: Disk scheduling orders I/O request queues to minimize disk arm seek time and rotational latency.
topics.whyItMatters: Calculating total head movement (cylinder tracks) for FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK, and C-LOOK is a standard numerical exam question.
understandSimply: Imagine an elevator servicing floors in a building.
SCAN (Elevator algorithm) goes all the way to the top floor, servicing requests on the way up, then reverses direction to go down.
C-SCAN goes up to the top floor servicing requests, then zooms straight down to the bottom floor without stopping, servicing only upward.
technicalExplanation: Disk Access Time components:
1. Seek Time: Time for disk arm to move read/write head to target cylinder track.
2. Rotational Latency: Time for target disk sector to rotate under head ($1/2 × Rotation Time$).
3. Transfer Time: Time to transfer data bytes (Data Size / Transfer Rate).
Disk Scheduling Algorithms:
First-Come, First-Served (FCFS): Services requests in queue arrival order. Wild head movement.
Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF): Services request closest to current head position. Minimizes seek time but can cause Starvation for distant tracks.
SCAN (Elevator): Arm moves in one direction to the end cylinder boundary of disk, servicing requests, then reverses direction.

C-SCAN (Circular SCAN): Arm moves in one direction to the end cylinder boundary, servicing requests, then immediately returns to cylinder 0 without servicing requests on the return trip. Provides uniform wait time.
LOOK / C-LOOK: Variants of SCAN/C-SCAN where the arm goes only as far as the LAST request in that direction, rather than all the way to the physical disk boundary.

definitions.definition: The time required for the hard disk read/write head assembly to move to the desired cylinder track.
The time taken for the requested sector of the disk platter to rotate under the read/write head.
Disk scheduling algorithm where the head travels from one end of the disk to the other, servicing requests along the way.
Circular SCAN scheduling where the head services requests in one direction only and returns to start without servicing.

steps.title: 1. Identify Request Queue & Start Position
steps.description: List request cylinder numbers, current head position, and disk boundaries (e.g. 0 to 199).

steps.title: 2. Sort Cylinder Requests
steps.description: Order cylinder numbers sequentially to easily trace head jumps.

steps.title: 3. Trace Head Traversal
steps.description: Follow specific algorithm path (e.g. SCAN moves toward 199 boundary, then reverses).

steps.title: 4. Sum Absolute Track Differences
steps.description: Total Seek Distance = Sum of |Current Position - Next Track Position| for all head moves.

formulasAndMethods: Total Head Movement = Sum(|Track_next - Track_current|)
Rotational Latency (Average) = 0.5 * (60 seconds / RPM)
Disk Access Time = Seek Time + Rotational Latency + Transfer Time
SCAN boundary rule: Arm travels all the way to cylinder 0 or Max (e.g., 199)
LOOK boundary rule: Arm travels only to min/max requested cylinder in queue

comparisons.title: SCAN vs C-SCAN Disk Scheduling
rows: Sweeps back and forth across entire disk width
Sweeps in one direction, then jumps back to start
Services requests in both inward and outward sweeps
Services requests in outward sweep only
Non-uniform wait times for edge tracks
Uniform wait time distribution for all tracks

comparisons.title: SCAN vs LOOK Disk Scheduling
rows: Head travels all the way to extreme disk boundary (0/max)
Head reverses direction at final pending request
Extra unproductive cylinder seeks at boundaries
Eliminates unnecessary cylinder seeks past last request

solvedExamples.question: A disk queue has requests for cylinders 98, 183, 37, 122. Current head is at 53. Under SSTF, what is the sequence of serviced cylinders?
solvedExamples.solution:
Current head = 53. Distances to [37, 98, 122, 183] from 53:
|53-37|=16, |53-98|=45, |53-122|=69, |53-183|=130.
1. Closest is 37 (head moves to 37).
From 37, remaining: 98 (dist 61), 122 (dist 85), 183 (dist 146).
2. Next closest is 98 (head moves to 98).
3. From 98, next closest is 122.
4. From 122, next closest is 183.
SSTF Sequence: 53 -> 37 -> 98 -> 122 -> 183.

solvedExamples.question: Consider a disk with cylinders 0 to 199. Request queue: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14. Initial head position = 53, moving TOWARD 199. Calculate total head movement using SCAN.
solvedExamples.solution:
In SCAN moving toward 199:
Head starts at 53, services higher requests in order: 98, 122, 183, then goes all the way to disk boundary 199.
Movement up = 199 - 53 = 146 tracks.
At 199, head reverses and services remaining lower requests: 37, 14.
Lowest request serviced is 14.
Movement down = 199 - 14 = 185 tracks.
Total Head Movement = 146 + 185 = 331 tracks.
(Alternatively: (199 - 53) + (199 - 14) = 331 tracks).

traps: SCAN goes all the way to the physical disk boundary (e.g. 0 or 199), whereas LOOK turns around at the last request.
In C-SCAN, the jump from end cylinder (199) back to start cylinder (0) counts as head movement (|199 - 0| = 199 tracks), but NO requests are serviced during that return trip.
Rotational Latency is based on RPM ($1/2 × (60 / RPM)$).
takeaways: SSTF minimizes seek time but can cause starvation.
SCAN (Elevator) goes to disk boundary; LOOK turns around at final request.
C-SCAN provides uniform wait time by servicing in one direction only.
Disk Access Time = Seek Time + Rotational Latency + Transfer Time.
Rotational Latency default = 0.5 / (RPM / 60).

quickRecall.question: What is the key difference between SCAN and LOOK disk scheduling?
quickRecall.answer: SCAN goes all the way to the physical disk boundary; LOOK turns around at the furthest request.

quickRecall.question: Which disk scheduling algorithm provides the most uniform wait time across cylinders?
quickRecall.answer: C-SCAN (Circular SCAN).

quickRecall.question: What is the average rotational latency for a 7200 RPM hard disk?

topics.title: File System Structure, Allocation Methods, and Directory Systems
topics.oneLine: File systems organize storage on disk using directory structures and block allocation schemes such as contiguous, linked, and indexed (i-node).
topics.whyItMatters: Calculating maximum file size in UNIX i-nodes (direct, single, double, triple indirect blocks) is a classic high-frequency GATE/IOCL exam problem.
understandSimply: Directory structures are like file folders.
Contiguous allocation is storing a document in 10 consecutive pages in a binder.
Linked allocation is a treasure hunt where page 1 tells you page 2 is on page 45.
Indexed allocation (i-node) is a table of contents page at the front listing exact page numbers for every section.
technicalExplanation: A File is a logical contiguous address space created by the OS over physical storage.
Directory Structures: Single-Level (name collisions), Two-Level (user subdirectories), Tree-Structured (path names), Acyclic-Graph (shared files via symlinks/hardlinks).
Allocation Methods:
1. Contiguous Allocation: File occupies consecutive disk blocks. Fast sequential/random access, but suffers from External Fragmentation and hard to grow files.

2. Linked Allocation: Each file is a linked list of disk blocks. Directory contains pointer to first and last block. Eliminates external fragmentation, but slow random access ($O(N)$) and pointer overhead.
3. Indexed Allocation: Brings all block pointers together into an Index Block (e.g. UNIX i-node). Supports direct random access ($O(1)$) without external fragmentation.
UNIX i-node Structure: Contains file metadata + Direct Pointers (e.g. 12) + 1 Single Indirect Pointer + 1 Double Indirect Pointer + 1 Triple Indirect Pointer.
Block Pointer Capacity = Block Size / Pointer Size.

definitions.definition: A Unix file system control structure holding file attributes and block pointers (direct and indirect).
A file allocation scheme requiring each file to occupy a set of contiguous blocks on disk.
A file allocation method where each file has its own index block storing array pointers to data blocks.
Hard link points directly to the file i-node; Soft link (symlink) is a special file containing path string to target.

steps.title: 1. Read Disk Block Size & Pointer Size
steps.description: Identify Disk Block Size $B$ bytes and Pointer Size $P$ bytes. Compute Pointers per Index Block $K = B / P$.

steps.title: 2. Count Direct Block Data Capacity
steps.description: Direct Capacity = Number of Direct Pointers $× B$.

steps.title: 3. Count Indirect Block Data Capacity
steps.description: Single Indirect = $K × B$; Double Indirect = $K^2 × B$; Triple Indirect = $K^3 × B$.

steps.title: 4. Sum Total Maximum File Size
steps.description: Max File Size = $(Direct + K + K^2 + K^3) × B$ bytes.

formulasAndMethods: Pointers Per Block (K) = Disk Block Size / Disk Pointer Size
Max Data Blocks in i-node = Direct_Count + K + K^2 + K^3
Max File Size = Max Data Blocks * Disk Block Size
Direct Block Limit Access = 1 disk access; Single Indirect = 2 disk accesses; Double Indirect = 3 disk accesses

comparisons.title: Contiguous vs Linked vs Indexed Allocation
rows: Zero external fragmentation; internal fragmentation on last block
Easy; allocates any free block in file system

comparisons.title: Hard Link vs Symbolic Link (Symlink)
rows: Points directly to target file's i-node
Independent file holding path string of target
Data remains until link count drops to 0
Dangling symlink if target file is deleted/moved

solvedExamples.question: A Unix file system has block size = 1 KB (1024 bytes) and disk pointer size = 4 bytes. An i-node has 12 direct pointers, 1 single indirect, 1 double indirect, and 1 triple indirect pointer. How many pointers can one index block hold?
solvedExamples.solution: Pointers per Block (K) = Block Size / Pointer Size = 1024 / 4 = 256 pointers.

solvedExamples.question: Using the i-node parameters above (Block Size = 1KB, K = 256), what is the maximum file size supported using up to double indirect pointers?
solvedExamples.solution:
Direct blocks = 12 blocks.
Single indirect blocks = 256 blocks.
Double indirect blocks = 256 * 256 = 65,536 blocks.
Total data blocks = 12 + 256 + 65,536 = 65,804 blocks.
Maximum File Size = 65,804 * 1 KB = 65,804 KB approx 64.26 MB.

traps: Pointers per block $K = Block Size / Pointer Size$, NOT pointer size / block size.
In UNIX i-node, reading a double-indirect block data byte requires 3 DISK ACCESSES (1 for single indirect level, 1 for double indirect level, 1 for actual data block).
Deleting the original file corrupts a Symbolic Link (soft link), but does NOT corrupt a Hard Link (hard link increments i-node reference count).
takeaways: Contiguous allocation has external fragmentation; Linked allocation has slow random access.
Indexed allocation (i-node) combines direct and multi-level indirect pointers.
Pointers per block $K = B / P$.
Max file size = $(Direct + K + K^2 + K^3) × B$.
Hard links point to i-nodes; Soft links point to path strings.

quickRecall.question: How many disk accesses are needed to read a data byte stored in a double-indirect block of an i-node?
quickRecall.answer: 3 disk accesses (1st indirect block + 2nd indirect block + data block).

quickRecall.question: What is the formula for pointers per block K given block size B and pointer size P?
quickRecall.answer: K = B / P.

quickRecall.question: Does deleting the target file break a hard link pointing to it?
quickRecall.answer: No. The i-node is retained until the hard link reference count becomes 0.
